section_summary: The Tokyo embassy reports the difficulty of translating Japan’s communications laws and asks which regulations the Federal Communications Commission needs. After an exchange with the Department of State and the Commission, the embassy sends translations of selected laws. This section contains four of those translations, covering telegraph and wireless services, foreign telegrams, ship communications, charges, and penalties; the remaining enclosures fall outside these pages.

people.name: Anning S. Prall
people.role: Chairman of the Federal Communications Commission

people.name: Wilbur J. Carr
people.role: Signed for the Secretary of State

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2244 on communications laws and regulations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The embassy reports that translating Japanese communications regulations will take considerable time and asks which are needed.
subfiles.summary: Grew encloses a list of laws and regulations and asks the Department and Federal Communications Commission to identify those they do not require translated.

subfiles.title: List of principal Japanese communications laws and regulations
subfiles.about: The enclosure lists communications laws and regulations in force in Japan as of January 1, 1937.
subfiles.summary: The list covers telegraphy, television, military communications, telephones, broadcasting, and international services, giving law or ordinance numbers and dates.

subfiles.title: Transmittal to the Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: The Department forwards Grew’s despatch and asks what reply to give about the proposed translations.
subfiles.summary: Forwards despatch No. 2244 and requests the Commission’s guidance.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on Tokyo despatch
subfiles.about: A brief internal note refers to Tokyo’s despatch No. 2244 and earlier embassy translations.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note; much of its wording is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Division of Far Eastern Affairs note on earlier translations
subfiles.about: An internal note appears to discuss communications laws already translated or received from other sources.
subfiles.summary: Handwritten note; most wording is illegible in the OCR.

subfiles.title: Federal Communications Commission acknowledgment
subfiles.from: Anning S. Prall, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: The Commission acknowledges the Japanese law list and promises to identify regulations it does not need.
subfiles.summary: Prall says the Commission will review the list and advise the Department promptly.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew on previous translations
subfiles.from: Department of State, signed by Wilbur J. Carr
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department relays the Commission’s response and points Grew to earlier translations of Japanese communications laws.
subfiles.summary: The Commission is reviewing the list. The Department cites earlier embassy despatches and a Japanese Embassy note containing translations already received.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2925 transmitting communications laws
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grew transmits seven translated Japanese communications laws and regulations.
subfiles.summary: The embassy lists seven enclosures, identifies three previously submitted translations, and says it regards the Department’s request as answered unless instructed otherwise.

subfiles.title: The Telegraph Law
subfiles.from: Japanese government; translated by American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The translated law governs telegraph and telephone facilities, service, fees, powers, and offenses.
subfiles.summary: The law provides for private installations, public and military use, restrictions for public safety, delivery and fees, and government access to land and railway property. It sets penalties for unauthorized facilities, breached secrecy, false messages, interference, and damage to lines.

subfiles.title: Wireless Telegraph Law
subfiles.from: Japanese government; translated by American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The translated law regulates wireless telegraph and telephone stations, licensing, public service, and offenses.
subfiles.summary: The law places wireless stations under government control while allowing licensed private stations for ships, enterprises, isolated locations, and experiments. Its later articles set penalties for unlicensed use, misuse, secrecy violations, false distress messages, and obstruction, and extend provisions to aircraft.

subfiles.title: Regulations Relating to Foreign Telegrams
subfiles.from: Japanese Ministry of Communications; translated by American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The ordinance sets rules for sending, charging for, and delivering foreign telegrams.
subfiles.summary: The regulations specify permissible writing, charges, prepayment, dispatch, delivery, press telegrams, and reduced rates. They also address Japanese-language telegram routes involving Shanghai and several Chinese cities, with supplementary provisions on earlier permits and regulations.

subfiles.title: Regulations Relating to Wireless Telegraph Messages
subfiles.from: Japanese Ministry of Communications; translated by American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The ordinance regulates wireless messages among shore, ship, fixed, and special stations.
subfiles.summary: The rules define station types and give priority to distress and navigation warnings. They govern ship and land messages, regular broadcasts, permission requirements, delivery, charges, refunds, and monthly payments. The supplementary rules replace earlier radio telegram regulations.
